title: The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali
summary: Some two hundred short threads of teaching on how to still the movements of the mind, so that pure awareness can rest in its own nature. They cover the states of samadhi, the eight-limbed practice, the powers that come along the way, and final freedom.

primer.a: 这是古印度讲瑜伽的经典，原文是梵文，一共一百九十多句短句，分成四品（四章）。传统上说编者是帕坦伽利，成书年代说法不一，一般认为在约两千年前到一千六百年前之间。它是印度六派正统哲学里瑜伽派的根本经典，不是佛经。书里的「瑜伽」主要不是体操，而是让心静下来的一整套方法，讲坐姿的只有两三句。
没有对话，也没有故事，从头到尾是作者一个人在一条一条地陈述，像一本教科书的要点。书里几乎没有「我」和「你」，主语常常省掉，本站在括号（）里补上。
这本书借用了数论派（印度另一派哲学）的看法：世界上有两样根本不同的东西。一样是原人，只是在「看」的纯粹意识；另一样是原质，会变出身体、心念和万物，由三德组成。人之所以受苦，是把这两样当成了一回事，把心里的起伏当成了自己。瑜伽要做的，就是让心静下来，看清两者的分别，最后让原人单独安住，这叫独存。

primer.q: 读的时候会卡住的地方
primer.a: 每一句都极短，原本是给学生背下来、再由老师讲解的提纲，所以单看一句常常不知所云，要连着前后几句读。同一样东西有好几个叫法：「观者」「原人」「纯粹意识」「真我」都指那个只看不动的意识。第三品列出很多特殊能力，比如知道前世、隐身、在空中走，本站照原文译出，不加评论。
这些词会反复出现，先认一下。
terms: 心的波动
心里一刻不停的起伏：认知、想象、做梦、回忆等等。瑜伽就是让它停下来。
原人、观者
只是在「看」、自己不动的纯粹意识，被看作人真正的自我。
原质
能变出身体、心念和一切事物的根源，和原人相对。
三德
原质的三种成分：明亮（萨埵）、活动、沉重静止。万物都由它们混合而成。
三昧
心完全专注在一个对象上、连自己都好像不见了的状态。
自在天
一位特殊的原人，从来不受烦恼和业的沾染，可以敬奉他来帮助修行。
烦恼
让人受苦的五种心病：无明、「我在」的感觉、贪爱、嗔恨、贪生怕死。
潜在印记
经历过的事在心里留下的痕迹，会在以后推动新的念头。
总制
专注、冥想、三昧三步合在同一个对象上。
独存
原人不再和心混在一起、单独安住在自己本来的样子，是全书的终点。

primer.a: 先读第一品「三昧品」的第 1 到 16 句：什么是瑜伽，心有哪五种波动，怎样靠练习和放下贪求让它停下来。再读第二品「修习品」的第 29 到 55 句，就是有名的「八支」，最贴近日常。接着回头读第二品前半（人为什么苦）和第三品「神通品」的前 8 句。第一品后半、第三品其余部分和第四品「独存品」最抽象，放到最后。每品先看「这一章在讲什么」。

primerEn.a: This is the classic Indian text on yoga, written in Sanskrit: about two hundred short lines in four books. Tradition names Patanjali as the compiler; its date is disputed, but it is generally placed somewhere between about two thousand and sixteen hundred years ago. It is the founding text of the Yoga school, one of the six orthodox schools of Indian philosophy, and not a Buddhist scripture. Its "yoga" is mostly not exercise but a whole method for quieting the mind; posture gets only two or three lines.

There is no dialogue and no story. From start to finish one author states his points one after another, like the outline of a textbook. There is almost no "I" or "you", and subjects are often left out.

The book borrows the view of the Samkhya school, another Indian philosophy: there are two utterly different things in the world. One is purusha, pure awareness that only watches. The other is nature (prakriti), which turns into body, mind and everything else and is made of three strands. People suffer because they mistake the two for one, taking the mind's ups and downs to be themselves. Yoga stills the mind, sees the difference, and in the end lets awareness rest alone; this is called aloneness.

Each line is extremely short. These were notes for students to memorize and for a teacher to explain, so one line on its own often makes little sense; read it with the lines around it. One thing can have several names: "the Seer", "purusha", "the true self" and "pure awareness" all mean the awareness that watches and does not move. Book 3 lists many special powers, such as knowing past lives, becoming invisible and walking in the air; they are translated as written, without comment.
These come up again and again.
terms: Fluctuations
The mind's constant movements: knowing, imagining, dreaming, remembering and so on. Yoga is their stilling.
Purusha, the Seer
Pure awareness that only watches and never moves, seen as a person's true self.
Nature (prakriti)
The source of body, mind and all things, the opposite of purusha.
The three strands
The three ingredients of nature: brightness, activity, and heaviness or inertia. Everything is some mix of them.
Samadhi
The state in which the mind is wholly absorbed in one object, as if it had disappeared itself.
Ishvara
The Lord: a special purusha never touched by afflictions or karma, to whom one may turn in devotion as an aid to practice.
Afflictions
The five ills that cause suffering: ignorance, the sense of "I am", attraction, aversion, and clinging to life.
Latent impressions
Traces that experiences leave in the mind, which later push up new thoughts.
Samyama
Concentration, meditation and samadhi together on a single object.
Aloneness
Awareness no longer mixed up with the mind, resting alone in its own nature; the goal of the whole book.

primerEn.a: Read lines 1 to 16 of Book 1 first: what yoga is, the mind's five kinds of fluctuation, and how practice and letting go of craving still them. Then lines 29 to 55 of Book 2, the well-known "eight limbs", the most down-to-earth part. Then go back to the first half of Book 2 (why people suffer) and the first eight lines of Book 3. Leave the rest of Book 1, the rest of Book 3, and Book 4, the most abstract parts, for last.

compare: 整部经的钥匙是第二句：yogaś cittavṛttinirodhaḥ。英文常见译法把 nirodha 译成 restraint 或 control，听起来像用力压住；本站英文写 stilling，白话写「止息」，都更接近「让波动自己平下来」。citta 也要小心：中文「心」同时是心脏、感情和思想，英文 mind 偏思考，而瑜伽经里的 citta 是一件属于物质的工具，真正的觉知者在它后面，叫 puruṣa。这一层在两种语言里都要读到后面才看得出来。

第二个大差别在「专注—冥想—三昧」这一组词。梵文 dhāraṇā、dhyāna、samādhi 是一步比一步深的三个阶段，合起来叫 saṃyama。英文 concentration、meditation 都是日常大词，meditation 尤其什么都能装；中文「禅」本身就是 dhyāna 的音译，「三昧」是 samādhi 的音译，带着佛教的联想。本站英文保留 samadhi、samyama 原词，再用 integrated focus 解释；白话用「专注、冥想、三昧、总制」，前两个好懂、后两个要靠注释。

第三是数论（Sāṃkhya）的一套专门词。puruṣa 字面就是「人」，白话沿用旧译「原人」，英文写 true self，但 self 容易被读成平常的自我；guṇa 原义是「一股绳子」，英文 strands 留住了这个画面，中文「三德」完全看不出来；kaivalya 来自「单独」，英文常译 liberation，本站写 aloneness，白话「独存」，都保留了「只剩自己」的意思：解脱不是去到哪里，而是观者不再和所观之物缠在一起。
第四，瑜伽经和佛教共用了大量词汇：kleśa（烦恼）、慈悲喜舍、四颠倒、寻与伺、刹那、法云、习气。中文读者看到这些熟悉的字，很容易把佛教的意思带进来；英文读者反而没有这层干扰。同一组「把非我当成我」，佛教的结论是「无我」，瑜伽经的结论却是「真我另在」，字面几乎一样，方向相反。
最后是文体。经文极简，常常只有主语和一个名词，靠注释家补全。白话用括号把补出来的字标出来，英文则把每一句展开成完整的句子，不加括号，所以两边的「补法」偶尔不同，比如「他说的话就会应验」「打开田埂放水」，白话按注释补了，英文只译到原文为止。另一个现代误读是 āsana：经里只有三句，讲的是能久坐冥想的坐姿，不是今天瑜伽课上的各种体式。
compareEn: The key to the whole text is the second sūtra: yogaś cittavṛttinirodhaḥ. Common English translations render nirodha as “restraint” or “control,” which sounds like forcibly holding something down; this site’s English says “stilling,” and the plain Chinese says 止息 (zhǐxī, “stilling, coming to rest”), both closer to “letting the ripples settle on their own.” Citta needs care too: the Chinese 心 (xīn) means the heart, the feelings and the thinking mind all at once, while English “mind” leans toward thinking. In the Yoga Sūtras, citta is an instrument that belongs to the material side of things; the real knower stands behind it and is called puruṣa. In both languages this only becomes clear once you read further.

The second big difference is the cluster “concentration, meditation, samādhi.” In Sanskrit, dhāraṇā, dhyāna and samādhi are three stages, each deeper than the last, and together they are called saṃyama. English “concentration” and “meditation” are broad everyday words, and “meditation” in particular can hold almost anything. In Chinese, 禅 (chán, the word behind Japanese “Zen”) is itself a transliteration of dhyāna, and 三昧 (sānmèi) is a transliteration of samādhi, both carrying Buddhist associations. This site’s English keeps the original words samadhi and samyama and explains the latter as “integrated focus”; the plain Chinese uses 专注 (zhuānzhù, “concentration”), 冥想 (míngxiǎng, “meditation”), 三昧 (sānmèi) and 总制 (zǒngzhì, an academic rendering of saṃyama). The first two are easy to understand; the last two need a note.

Third is the specialist vocabulary of Sāṃkhya philosophy. Puruṣa literally means “person”; the plain Chinese keeps the old rendering 原人 (yuánrén, “original person”), while the English says “true self,” though “self” is easily read as the ordinary ego. Guṇa originally means “a strand of rope”; the English “strands” keeps that picture, while the Chinese 三德 (sāndé, “the three qualities”) loses it completely. Kaivalya comes from a word for “alone”; English often translates it as “liberation,” but this site says “aloneness,” and the plain Chinese says 独存 (dúcún, “existing alone”). Both keep the sense of “only oneself remaining”: liberation is not going somewhere, but the seer no longer being tangled up with what is seen.

Fourth, the Yoga Sūtras share a great deal of vocabulary with Buddhism: kleśa, rendered 烦恼 (fánnǎo, “afflictions, vexations”); the four attitudes 慈悲喜舍 (cí bēi xǐ shě, “friendliness, compassion, gladness, equanimity”); the four inversions 四颠倒 (sì diāndǎo); 寻 and 伺 (xún and sì, “coarse thought and subtle reflection”); 刹那 (chànà, “instant”); 法云 (fǎyún, “cloud of dharma”); and 习气 (xíqì, “habit-energies”). Chinese readers who see these familiar words easily bring Buddhist meanings along with them; English readers, oddly, are spared that interference. The same list of mistakes ends in “taking the non-self for the self,” yet Buddhism concludes there is no self, while the Yoga Sūtras conclude that the true self lies elsewhere: almost identical wording, opposite direction.

Finally, style. The sūtras are extremely terse, often just a subject and a noun, and rely on commentators to fill them out. The plain Chinese puts the supplied words in parentheses, while the English expands each sūtra into a full sentence without brackets, so the two sometimes fill the gaps differently. For example, “what he says comes true” and “opening the field ridge to let the water through” are supplied in the plain Chinese following the commentaries, while the English translates only as far as the original goes. Another modern misreading concerns āsana: the text gives it only three sūtras, and it means a seated posture you can hold for long meditation, not the range of poses taught in yoga classes today.

chapters.title: Book 1 · On Samadhi
chapters.intro: It opens with a definition: yoga is the stilling of the mind's fluctuations, and then the Seer, pure awareness, rests in its own nature. It lists five kinds of fluctuation, stilled by steady practice and letting go of craving, or by devotion to Ishvara and repeating Om. The second half describes ever deeper stages of samadhi.

verses.en: Now begins the teaching of yoga.

cmp.note: 字面是「随后的教导」，anu 有「跟着、承接」的意思，暗示这是接续前人的传授，不是帕坦伽利自创。英文 teaching、白话「讲授」都看不出「承接」这一层。
cmp.en: Literally “the teaching that follows”: anu means “after, following on,” hinting that this continues an earlier line of teaching rather than being Patañjali’s own invention. Neither the English “teaching” nor the plain Chinese 讲授 (jiǎngshòu, “to teach, lecture”) shows this sense of carrying on a tradition.

verses.en: Yoga is the stilling of the mind's fluctuations.

cmp.note: 中文「心」同时指心脏、情感和思想，英文 mind 偏向思考。瑜伽经里的 citta 是整套心理机能，而且属于物质那一边，不是真正的觉知者；这一点英文、中文都表达不出来，要读到后面才明白。
cmp.en: The Chinese 心 (xīn) means the heart, the emotions and thought all at once, while English “mind” leans toward thinking. In the Yoga Sūtras, citta is the whole mental apparatus, and it belongs to the material side, not to the true knower; neither English nor Chinese can express this, and it only becomes clear later in the text.

cmp.note: 原义是「转动、运作」。英文 fluctuations、白话「波动」都用水面起伏来比喻；梵文本身没有水的意象，只是说心「在运转」。
cmp.en: The root meaning is “turning, functioning.” The English “fluctuations” and the plain Chinese 波动 (bōdòng, “waves, rippling”) both use the image of a rippling water surface; the Sanskrit itself has no water imagery and simply says the mind is “in operation.”

cmp.note: 英文常见译法 restraint、control 带着「用力压住」的意思；本站英文写 stilling，白话写「止息」，都更接近「让波动自己平下来」。这个词决定了整部经的基调。
cmp.en: Common English renderings like “restraint” or “control” suggest forcibly holding something down. This site’s English says “stilling” and the plain Chinese says 止息 (zhǐxī, “stilling, coming to rest”), both closer to letting the ripples settle on their own. This one word sets the tone for the whole text.

verses.en: Then the Seer rests in its own true nature.

cmp.note: 「看的人」。英文 Seer、白话「观者」都照字面；它指的是纯粹意识（原人），不是用眼睛看东西的那个「我」。
cmp.en: “The one who sees.” The English “Seer” and the plain Chinese 观者 (guānzhě, “the observer”) are both literal; it refers to pure consciousness (puruṣa), not the “I” that looks at things with its eyes.

verses.en: At other times, the Seer takes on the look of the fluctuations.

cmp.note: 「形态相同」，只是看起来一样，并不真的变成波动。英文 takes on the look of、白话「看起来是同一个样子」都保留了「只是看起来」这层分寸。
cmp.en: “Sameness of form”: it only looks the same, without actually turning into the fluctuations. The English “takes on the look of” and the plain Chinese 看起来是同一个样子 (kàn qǐlái shì tóng yī gè yàngzi, “looks like the same thing”) both keep this careful “only seems” nuance.

verses.en: The fluctuations are of five kinds, some afflicted and some not.

cmp.note: 由 kleśa（烦恼）而来，意思是「被烦恼染上、会带来麻烦的」，不一定当下就痛苦。英文 afflicted 和白话「带烦恼的」都可以，但读者容易以为是「让人难受的」念头。
cmp.en: Derived from kleśa (affliction), it means “stained by the afflictions, bound to cause trouble,” not necessarily painful in the moment. The English “afflicted” and the plain Chinese 带烦恼的 (dài fánnǎo de, “carrying afflictions”) both work, but readers may assume it means thoughts that feel unpleasant.

verses.en: They are: valid knowing, error, imagination, sleep, and memory.

cmp.note: 指只靠语言撑起来、没有真实对象的念头。英文 imagination 偏「幻想」，白话「概念想象」更准；佛教汉译常把同一个词译成「分别」，意思又不完全一样。
cmp.en: A thought held up only by words, with no real object behind it. The English “imagination” leans toward fantasy; the plain Chinese 概念想象 (gàiniàn xiǎngxiàng, “conceptual imagining”) is more precise. Buddhist Chinese translations often render the same word as 分别 (fēnbié, “discrimination, conceptualizing”), which does not mean quite the same thing.

verses.en: Valid knowing comes from direct perception, inference, and reliable testimony.
Error is false knowledge, resting on a form that does not match the thing itself.
Imagination is a thought that follows from words and ideas but has no real thing behind it.
Sleep is the fluctuation that rests on the experience of nothing at all.

cmp.note: 瑜伽经把无梦的深睡也算成一种心的波动，因为醒来时我们知道「刚才睡得什么都不知道」。英文 sleep、中文「睡眠」听起来像心停了，原文的意思正好相反。
cmp.en: The Yoga Sūtras count even dreamless deep sleep as a fluctuation of the mind, because on waking we know “I slept and knew nothing.” The English “sleep” and the Chinese 睡眠 (shuìmián, “sleep”) sound as if the mind has stopped, which is the opposite of what the original means.

verses.en: Memory is not letting slip something once experienced.
They are stilled through steady practice and letting go.

cmp.note: 由 rāga（染色、激情）加上「离开」构成，字面是「褪色」。英文常译 dispassion 或 non-attachment，本站写 letting go；白话「离欲」借佛教用语，偏重「离开欲望」，少了「颜色褪去」的画面。
cmp.en: Built from rāga (coloring, passion) plus “away from,” literally “fading of color.” English usually gives “dispassion” or “non-attachment,” and this site says “letting go”; the plain Chinese 离欲 (líyù, “leaving desire”) borrows a Buddhist term that stresses leaving desire behind and loses the picture of color draining away.

verses.en: Of the two, practice is the effort to stay steady there.
And practice becomes firmly grounded when it is kept up for a long time, without a break, and with devotion.
Letting go is the sense of mastery in someone who no longer thirsts for objects, whether seen or only heard of in sacred tradition.

cmp.note: 「从传承里听来的」，指吠陀经典描述的天界享乐。英文 heard of in sacred tradition、白话「从经典听来的」都只能简单交代，原文是在说连死后升天的福报也不再渴求。
cmp.en: “Heard from tradition,” referring to the heavenly pleasures described in the Vedic scriptures. The English “heard of in sacred tradition” and the plain Chinese 从经典听来的 (cóng jīngdiǎn tīng lái de, “heard from the scriptures”) can only state this briefly; the original is saying that one no longer craves even the reward of going to heaven after death.

verses.en: Higher than that is having no thirst even for the strands of nature themselves, which comes from seeing the true self, purusha.

cmp.note: 字面就是「人」。白话沿用旧译「原人」，英文写 true self / purusha。它在数论和瑜伽里指纯粹的觉知，不思考、不行动，只是「看」；英文 self 容易被读成平常的「自我」。
cmp.en: Literally just “person.” The plain Chinese keeps the old rendering 原人 (yuánrén, “original person”); the English says “true self” or purusha. In Sāṃkhya and Yoga it means pure awareness, which does not think or act but only “sees”; the English “self” is easily read as the ordinary ego.

cmp.note: 原义是「一股绳子」。物质世界被看成由三股绳拧成：明亮（sattva）、活动（rajas）、沉滞（tamas）。英文 strands 保留了绳子的画面；中文「三德」「性质」都看不出来。
cmp.en: Originally “a strand of rope.” The material world is pictured as three strands twisted together: brightness (sattva), activity (rajas) and inertia (tamas). The English “strands” keeps the rope image; the Chinese 三德 (sāndé, “three qualities”) and 性质 (xìngzhì, “properties”) show none of it.

verses.en: Samadhi with awareness of an object comes with coarse thought, subtle reflection, joy, and the bare sense of "I am."

cmp.note: 本义是「放在一起、合拢」，指心完全沉进对象的状态。英文常译 concentration 或 absorption，前者太浅；中文「三昧」是音译，不懂的人看不出意思，懂的人又会带入佛教的联想。本站英文直接用 samadhi。
cmp.en: The root meaning is “putting together, joining,” the state in which the mind is fully absorbed in its object. English often gives “concentration” or “absorption,” the former too shallow; the Chinese 三昧 (sānmèi) is a transliteration of samādhi borrowed from Buddhism, opaque to those who don’t know it and loaded with Buddhist associations for those who do. This site’s English simply uses samadhi.

cmp.note: 白话译「寻」「伺」，借的是佛教禅定术语；英文写 coarse thought、subtle reflection，用粗细来区分，比「寻、伺」两个字好懂。
cmp.en: The plain Chinese renders these as 寻 (xún, “searching”) and 伺 (sì, “watching”), borrowed from Buddhist meditation terminology; the English “coarse thought” and “subtle reflection” distinguish them by coarse versus fine, which is easier to grasp than those two single characters.

verses.en: The other kind follows on practicing the thought of stopping; in it only latent impressions remain.

cmp.note: 经验留在心底的痕迹，日后会再冒出来。英文 latent impressions、白话「潜在印记」都是意译；佛教汉译常把同一个词译成「行」，那个意思宽得多，读瑜伽经时别混在一起。
cmp.en: The traces experience leaves deep in the mind, which later resurface. The English “latent impressions” and the plain Chinese 潜在印记 (qiánzài yìnjì, “latent imprints”) are both interpretive; Buddhist Chinese often renders the same word as 行 (xíng, “formations”), a much broader meaning, so don’t mix them up when reading the Yoga Sūtras.

verses.en: For those who are bodiless, or merged into nature, it arises from the state of being they are born into.

cmp.note: 「以存在状态为因」。白话写「是他们的存在状态带来的，生来就有」，英文写 the state of being they are born into；原文本身很简略，注释家多解释成前世修行的结果，白话没有把这层补进去。
cmp.en: “Caused by the state of being.” The plain Chinese says 是他们的存在状态带来的，生来就有 (“it comes from their state of being; they are born with it”), and the English “the state of being they are born into”; the original is very brief. Commentators usually explain it as the result of practice in a previous life, which the plain Chinese does not add.

verses.en: For others, it comes after faith, energy, mindfulness, samadhi, and insight.

cmp.note: 这里的 smṛti 是「正念、持续记得修行」。同一个词在前面是「记忆」这种心的波动；英文和白话都按上下文换了译法，读者看不出原文是同一个字。
cmp.en: Here smṛti means mindfulness, continually remembering one’s practice. Earlier the same word meant “memory,” one of the mind’s fluctuations; the English and the plain Chinese both switch renderings by context, so readers can’t tell it is the same word in the original.

verses.en: For those with an intense urgency, it is near.
And it differs further depending on whether that urgency is mild, moderate, or intense.
Or it comes through devotion to Ishvara, the Lord.

cmp.note: 字面是「主宰者」。白话「自在天」在汉译佛经里多指湿婆一类的大神，容易让人以为是某位特定的神；瑜伽经里的 Ishvara 只是一个特别的原人，没有创世的角色。英文 the Lord 也带着基督教的味道。
cmp.en: Literally “the ruler.” The plain Chinese 自在天 (zìzàitiān, “the sovereign god”) in Chinese Buddhist scriptures usually refers to a great god like Śiva, which may suggest one particular deity; in the Yoga Sūtras, Ishvara is simply a special puruṣa with no role in creating the world. The English “the Lord” also carries a Christian flavor.

cmp.note: 「把自己放到…面前、交托」。英文 devotion、白话「虔诚敬奉」偏重感情；原文还有「把行为的结果交出去」的意思。
cmp.en: “Placing oneself before, entrusting.” The English “devotion” and the plain Chinese 虔诚敬奉 (qiánchéng jìngfèng, “pious worship”) lean toward emotion; the original also carries the sense of handing over the fruits of one’s actions.

verses.en: Ishvara is a special kind of self, untouched by afflictions, by actions, by their ripening, or by their stored traces.
In Ishvara the seed of all-knowing is unsurpassed.
Not being limited by time, Ishvara is the teacher even of the earliest teachers.
The word that expresses Ishvara is the sacred syllable, Om.

cmp.note: 原文只说 praṇava（「神圣的嗡鸣声」），没有直接写出 Om。英文和白话都把注释家公认的「唵／Om」补了进去。
cmp.en: The original says only praṇava (“the sacred humming sound”) and does not actually write Om. Both the English and the plain Chinese supply “Om” (Chinese 唵, ǎn), as the commentators agree it means.

verses.en: Repeat it, and dwell on what it means.
From this comes the discovery of inward awareness, and the obstacles fall away.
Illness, dullness, doubt, carelessness, laziness, craving, wrong views, failing to reach a stage, and failing to stay in it: these scatter the mind, and they are the obstacles.
Along with this scattering come pain, low spirits, trembling of the body, and uneven breathing in and out.
To counter them, practice on a single principle.

cmp.note: 「单一的真实、单一的原理」。白话写「单一的对象」，英文写 a single principle；注释家对这里到底指一个对象还是指 Ishvara 有争论，两种译法各自偏了一边。
cmp.en: “A single reality, a single principle.” The plain Chinese says 单一的对象 (dānyī de duìxiàng, “a single object”), the English “a single principle”; commentators disagree over whether this means one object or Ishvara, and each rendering leans to one side.

verses.en: The mind becomes clear by cultivating friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward those who suffer, gladness toward the virtuous, and equanimity toward those without virtue.

cmp.note: 这四种心和佛教的「慈、悲、喜、舍」是同一组词。中文读者一看就熟，英文 friendliness、compassion、gladness、equanimity 则是一般用语。upekṣā 不是冷漠，而是「不起反感、不被牵动」。
cmp.en: These four attitudes are the same set of words as Buddhism’s 慈悲喜舍 (cí bēi xǐ shě, “loving-kindness, compassion, joy, equanimity”), instantly familiar to Chinese readers, whereas the English “friendliness, compassion, gladness, equanimity” are ordinary words. Upekṣā is not indifference; it means not reacting with aversion and not being pulled along.

verses.en: Or by breathing out and holding the breath.

cmp.note: 既是呼吸，也是生命力。白话写「气息」，英文写 breath，都只取了呼吸那一面。
cmp.en: Both breath and life-force. The plain Chinese 气息 (qìxī, “breath”) and the English “breath” both capture only the breathing side.

verses.en: Or a refined sense experience, once it arises, ties the mind down to steadiness.
Or a state free of sorrow and full of light.
Or a mind that takes as its object someone free of desire.
Or one that rests on what is known in dreams or in deep sleep.
Or by meditating on whatever one likes.
Such a person's mastery reaches from the tiniest particle to the very largest.

When the fluctuations have worn away, the mind becomes like a flawless crystal: whatever it rests on, whether the knower, the act of knowing, or the thing known, it settles there and takes on its color. This is merging.

cmp.note: 「完全落到一起」。白话沿用佛教旧译「等至」，一般读者看不懂，所以在括号里补了「心和对象合一」；英文 merging 直接说出了心和对象合在一起的意思。
cmp.en: “Falling completely together.” The plain Chinese keeps the old Buddhist rendering 等至 (děngzhì, roughly “arriving at evenness”), which ordinary readers can’t follow, so it adds 心和对象合一 (“mind and object become one”) in brackets; the English “merging” says directly that the mind and its object come together.

verses.en: Of these, the merging that is mixed with the tangle of word, meaning, and idea is called merging with thought.
When memory is purified, and the mind seems emptied of its own form so that only the object shines through, it is called merging beyond thought.

cmp.note: 「好像空掉了自身的形态」。这里的 śūnya 和《心经》的「空」是同一个词，但意思很具体：心忘了自己，只剩对象。白话写「好像连自己的样子都空掉了」，留着「空」字，但说的是心忘了自己的样子，不是什么都没有。
cmp.en: “As if emptied of its own form.” The śūnya here is the same word as the 空 (kōng, “emptiness”) of the Heart Sūtra, but the meaning is concrete: the mind forgets itself and only the object remains. The plain Chinese 好像连自己的样子都空掉了 (“as if even its own shape had emptied out”) keeps the word 空 but makes clear it is the mind’s own shape that drops away, not that nothing exists.

verses.en: In the same way, merging with reflection and beyond reflection, which take subtle things as their objects, are also explained.
Subtle objects go all the way back to the unmarked, the unmanifest root of nature.
All of these are samadhi with a seed.

cmp.note: 「带着种子」。种子指还留在心里、日后会发芽的印记。英文 with a seed 和白话「有种子」都照字面，读者要知道「种子」在这里是比喻。
cmp.en: “With a seed.” The seed is an impression still lodged in the mind that will sprout later. The English “with a seed” and the plain Chinese 有种子 (yǒu zhǒngzi, “having a seed”) are both literal; readers need to know the seed is a metaphor here.

verses.en: When the state beyond reflection becomes clear and assured, an inner clarity dawns.
There, insight is truth-bearing.

cmp.note: ṛta 是吠陀里的「宇宙秩序、真理」。英文 truth-bearing、白话「承载真理的」都照字面译，但 ṛta 那层「天地本来的秩序」读不出来。
cmp.en: Ṛta is the Vedic “cosmic order, truth.” The English “truth-bearing” and the plain Chinese 承载真理的 (chéngzài zhēnlǐ de, “carrying truth”) are both literal, but the layer of ṛta as “the natural order of heaven and earth” doesn’t come through.

verses.en: Its object differs from that of what is learned by hearing or by inference, because it grasps the particular.
The impression born of it blocks other impressions.
When even that is stilled, everything is stilled, and this is seedless samadhi.

chapters.title: Book 2 · On Practice
chapters.intro: How to practise. First, why people suffer: five afflictions, rooted in ignorance, which mistakes the Seer for the mind. Then the eight limbs of yoga, with the first five explained in detail: restraints toward others, observances for oneself, posture, breath control, and drawing the senses inward.

verses.en: Austerity, self-study, and devotion to Ishvara together make up the yoga of action.

cmp.note: 本义是「热」，指修行时烧掉杂质的那股热力。白话「苦行」让人想到折磨身体，英文 austerity 也偏严苛；原文的重点是「炼」，不一定是「苦」。
cmp.en: The root meaning is “heat,” the heat of practice that burns away impurities. The plain Chinese 苦行 (kǔxíng, “ascetic hardship”) suggests mortifying the body, and the English “austerity” also leans severe; the point of the original is refining, not necessarily suffering.

cmp.note: 「自己的诵读」，原指反复诵读经典与真言。英文 self-study、白话「自我研读」容易被读成「研究自己」，其实是读经。
cmp.en: “One’s own recitation,” originally the repeated chanting of scripture and mantras. The English “self-study” and the plain Chinese 自我研读 (zìwǒ yándú, “self-study”) are easily read as “studying oneself,” when it actually means studying scripture.

verses.en: Its purpose is to bring about samadhi and to wear down the afflictions.
The afflictions are ignorance, the sense of "I am," attraction, aversion, and clinging to life.

cmp.note: 中文「烦恼」借自佛教，听起来像日常的烦心事；英文 afflictions 偏「病痛」。原文指让人一再受苦的根本心病，五种都是结构性的，不是情绪。
cmp.en: The Chinese 烦恼 (fánnǎo, “vexations”) is borrowed from Buddhism and sounds like everyday worries; the English “afflictions” leans toward illness. The original means the root sicknesses of the mind that cause suffering again and again; all five are structural, not emotions.

cmp.note: 字面是「执着、陷进去」，这里专指对活下去的执着。白话译「贪生怕死」很生动，但多了一点贬义；英文 clinging to life 比较中性。
cmp.en: Literally “clinging, sinking into,” here specifically clinging to staying alive. The plain Chinese 贪生怕死 (tānshēng pàsǐ, “greedy for life and afraid of death”) is vivid but adds a slightly pejorative tone; the English “clinging to life” is more neutral.

verses.en: Ignorance is the field for the others, whether they lie dormant, are worn thin, are held off for a while, or are in full force.
Ignorance is taking the impermanent for the permanent, the impure for the pure, suffering for happiness, and what is not the self for the self.

cmp.note: 这四种颠倒和佛教的「四颠倒」几乎一字不差，中文读者会觉得眼熟。但佛教说「无我」，瑜伽经的「非我」是说：心和身体不是真我（原人），真我另有所在。同一组词，结论相反。
cmp.en: These four inversions match Buddhism’s 四颠倒 (sì diāndǎo, “four inversions”) almost word for word, so Chinese readers will find them familiar. But Buddhism concludes there is no self, while the Yoga Sūtras’ “not-self” means that mind and body are not the true self (puruṣa), which exists elsewhere. The same words, opposite conclusions.

verses.en: The sense of "I am" is treating the power of seeing and the instrument of seeing as if they were one self.

cmp.note: 由「我是」（asmi）加抽象词尾而成。白话写成「我在」的感觉，英文写 the sense of "I am"；它不是骄傲，而是把心误当成真我的那种认同感。
cmp.en: Formed from “I am” (asmi) plus an abstract-noun ending. The plain Chinese writes 「我在」的感觉 (“wǒ zài” de gǎnjué, “the feeling of ‘I am’”), the English “the sense of ‘I am’”; it is not pride, but the identification that mistakes the mind for the true self.

verses.en: Attraction follows on pleasure.
Aversion follows on pain.
Clinging to life flows on by its own momentum, and it is rooted this way even in the wise.
In their subtle form, these are to be overcome by tracing them back to where they came from.

cmp.note: 「逆着生出来的方向回去」，让心回流到源头而消融。英文 tracing them back、白话「逆向回溯」都译出了方向，但原文更像「倒着生一遍」。
cmp.en: “Going back against the direction of birth,” letting the mind flow back to its source and dissolve. The English “tracing them back” and the plain Chinese 逆向回溯 (nìxiàng huísù, “tracing back in reverse”) both convey the direction, but the original is more like “being born again in reverse.”

verses.en: Their active fluctuations are to be overcome by meditation.
The store of karma, rooted in the afflictions, is felt in this visible life or in lives not yet seen.
As long as the root is there, it ripens into one's birth, length of life, and experience.
These bear the fruit of delight or anguish, depending on whether their cause was merit or wrongdoing.

For one who discerns, everything is simply suffering: because of the suffering of change, of anxiety, and of lingering impressions, and because the movements of the strands of nature clash with one another.

cmp.note: 英文 suffering、中文「苦」都很重。duḥkha 原义更像「不顺、卡住」，包括隐约的不满足。说「一切皆苦」不是说时时痛苦，而是说没有一样能让人真正安顿。
cmp.en: The English “suffering” and the Chinese 苦 (kǔ, “bitterness, suffering”) are both heavy. Duḥkha originally means something closer to “not running smoothly, stuck,” including a vague dissatisfaction. Saying “everything is suffering” doesn’t mean constant pain, but that nothing can bring true rest.

verses.en: What is to be avoided is suffering that has not yet come.
The cause of what is to be avoided is the joining of the seer and the seen.
The seen has the nature of brightness, activity, and inertia; it is made of the elements and the senses; and it exists for the sake of experience and of freedom.

cmp.note: 这三项就是三股「绳」：明亮、活动、沉滞，但原文没有点名。英文和白话都照字面译，读者若没注意到前面讲「三股绳」的那一句，未必知道这里在讲三德。
cmp.en: These three are the three “strands” (brightness, activity, inertia), but the original doesn’t name them as such. The English and the plain Chinese both translate literally, so readers who missed the earlier sūtra about the three strands may not realize the guṇas are meant here.

verses.en: The levels of the strands are: the specific, the unspecific, the merely marked, and the unmarked.
The seer is pure seeing alone; though pure, it looks on through the ideas in the mind.
The very being of the seen is only for the seer's sake.
For one whose purpose is fulfilled, the seen has vanished; yet it has not vanished, because it is shared with others.
The joining is what allows the powers of the owner and of what is owned to be known as they truly are.
Its cause is ignorance.
When ignorance is gone, the joining is gone. That is the letting go, the seer's aloneness.

cmp.note: 由 kevala（单独、唯一）而来，字面是「只剩自己」。英文常译 liberation，本站写 aloneness；白话「独存」也保留了「单独」。原文的解脱不是到达某处，而是观者不再和所观之物缠在一起。
cmp.en: From kevala (alone, sole), literally “only oneself remaining.” English often translates it as “liberation”; this site says “aloneness,” and the plain Chinese 独存 (dúcún, “existing alone”) also keeps the sense of being alone. Liberation in the original is not arriving somewhere, but the seer no longer being tangled up with what is seen.

verses.en: The means of letting go is unwavering discriminating insight.

cmp.note: 「看清分别」：看清原人和心是两回事。白话「分辨智」、英文 discriminating insight 都对，但英文 discriminating 在今天常让人想到「歧视」。
cmp.en: “Seeing the distinction clearly”: seeing that puruṣa and the mind are two different things. The plain Chinese 分辨智 (fēnbiàn zhì, “wisdom of discernment”) and the English “discriminating insight” are both correct, but “discriminating” today often brings to mind discrimination against people.

verses.en: For such a person, insight at its final stage has seven levels.
By practicing the limbs of yoga, impurity wears away, and the light of knowledge shines until discriminating insight arises.
Restraints, observances, posture, breath control, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, and samadhi are the eight limbs.

cmp.note: 「肢体」。英文 limbs 保留了身体的比喻：八支像一个人的四肢，同时存在，不只是八级台阶；白话「支分」比较抽象。
cmp.en: “Limbs.” The English “limbs” keeps the bodily metaphor: the eight limbs exist together like a person’s arms and legs, not just eight steps on a staircase. The plain Chinese 支分 (zhīfēn, “branches, components”) is more abstract.

cmp.note: yama 是「约束、不做什么」，niyama 是「要养成的习惯」。白话沿用「禁戒」「劝制」，英文写 restraints、observances，都把一组「对外」、一组「对己」的分别译了出来。
cmp.en: Yama means “restraint, what not to do,” niyama “habits to cultivate.” The plain Chinese keeps the traditional 禁戒 (jìnjiè, “prohibitions”) and 劝制 (quànzhì, “recommended disciplines”), the English “restraints” and “observances”; both convey the split between one set aimed outward and one aimed at oneself.

verses.en: The restraints are: not harming, truthfulness, not stealing, sexual restraint, and not grasping.

cmp.note: 字面是「在梵中行走」，原指学生时期的独身修行。白话「梵行」保留字面，英文 sexual restraint 只译出实际内容；后世解释从完全禁欲到节制不等。
cmp.en: Literally “walking in Brahman,” originally the celibate discipline of a student’s years. The plain Chinese 梵行 (fànxíng, “Brahmic conduct”) keeps the literal sense, while the English “sexual restraint” translates only the practical content; later interpretations range from total celibacy to moderation.

cmp.note: 「不抓取、不囤积」。白话「不贪占」偏道德；英文 not grasping 更接近原文「不往自己身边拢东西」。
cmp.en: “Not grasping, not hoarding.” The plain Chinese 不贪占 (bù tānzhàn, “not greedily possessing”) leans moral; the English “not grasping” is closer to the original sense of not pulling things toward oneself.

verses.en: When they are not limited by birth, place, time, or circumstance, and hold at every level, they are the great vow.

cmp.note: 指出身、种姓。注释家举的例子是渔夫：职业要杀鱼，就以为「不伤害」不适用于自己。原文的意思是不准用身份来打折扣。
cmp.en: Refers to birth and caste. The commentators’ example is a fisherman who, since his trade requires killing fish, assumes non-harming doesn’t apply to him. The original means one may not use one’s station to make exceptions.

verses.en: The observances are: cleanliness, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to Ishvara.
When unwholesome thoughts press in, cultivate their opposite.

cmp.note: 在第一章，vitarka 是三昧里「粗的寻思」；到这里却是「邪念」，指想去伤害、偷盗之类的念头。同一个词意思完全不同，英文和白话都只能换词来译。
cmp.en: In Chapter 1, vitarka was the “coarse thought” within samādhi; here it means “unwholesome thoughts,” the urge to harm, steal and so on. The same word has a completely different meaning, and both the English and the plain Chinese (邪念, xiéniàn, “wicked thoughts”) can only handle it by switching words.

verses.en: Unwholesome thoughts, such as harming, whether done, caused to be done, or approved of; whether arising from greed, anger, or delusion; whether mild, moderate, or intense, bear endless fruit in suffering and ignorance. Thinking this way is cultivating the opposite.
When someone is firmly grounded in not harming, others give up their hostility in that person's presence.
When someone is firmly grounded in truthfulness, actions and their results rest on that person's word.

cmp.note: 原文只说「行为与结果以他为依」。白话补出「他说的话就会应验」，是注释家的解释；英文只译到 rest on that person's word 为止。
cmp.en: The original says only “actions and results rest on him.” The plain Chinese adds 他说的话就会应验 (tā shuō de huà jiù huì yìngyàn, “what he says comes true”), which is the commentators’ interpretation; the English goes only as far as “rest on that person’s word.”

verses.en: When someone is firmly grounded in not stealing, every treasure comes to them.
When someone is firmly grounded in sexual restraint, vigor is gained.

cmp.note: 既是「勇气、精力」，也有「精液」的意思，注释家常从保存精气来解释。英文 vigor、白话「精力」都取了较宽的一面。
cmp.en: It means “courage, energy” and also “semen,” and commentators often explain it as conserving vital essence. The English “vigor” and the plain Chinese 精力 (jīnglì, “energy”) both take the broader sense.

verses.en: When not grasping becomes steady, one comes to understand the how and why of one's births.
From cleanliness comes a distaste for one's own body and no wish for contact with others.

cmp.note: 是很强的词：「厌恶、嫌弃」。英文 distaste 已经放轻了，白话「厌离」借佛教用语更软。原文意思是越讲究清净，越看清身体本来不干净。
cmp.en: A strong word: “disgust, revulsion.” The English “distaste” already softens it, and the plain Chinese 厌离 (yànlí, “weariness and turning away”), borrowed from Buddhism, is softer still. The point is that the more one cultivates purity, the more clearly one sees the body as inherently unclean.

verses.en: And also purity of being, cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery of the senses, and fitness to see the self.
From contentment comes unsurpassed happiness.
Through austerity, impurity wears away, and the body and senses reach perfection.
Through self-study comes union with one's chosen deity.
Through devotion to Ishvara comes the perfection of samadhi.
Posture should be steady and comfortable.

cmp.note: 本义是「座位、坐的方式」。整部经讲 āsana 只有三句，指的是能长时间安坐冥想的坐姿。英文 posture、中文「体式」在今天会让人想到瑜伽课上的各种姿势，那是后世才发展出来的。白话「坐法」「坐姿」更接近原意。
cmp.en: The root meaning is “seat, way of sitting.” The whole text spends only three sūtras on āsana, and it means a seated posture you can hold for long meditation. The English “posture” and the Chinese 体式 (tǐshì, “yoga pose”) today evoke the many poses of a yoga class, which developed much later; the plain Chinese 坐法 (zuòfǎ, “way of sitting”) and 坐姿 (zuòzī, “sitting posture”) are closer to the original.

verses.en: This comes through relaxing effort and letting the mind merge with the endless.

cmp.note: 「无尽」。注释家常解释成托着大地的神蛇 Ananta，意思是像它那样稳。英文 the endless、白话「无限」都取抽象义，没有那条蛇。
cmp.en: “Endless.” Commentators often explain it as Ananta, the divine serpent who holds up the earth, meaning steady as he is. The English “the endless” and the plain Chinese 无限 (wúxiàn, “infinity”) both take the abstract meaning, without the serpent.

verses.en: From this, one is no longer struck by the pairs of opposites.
Once posture is in place, breath control is the pausing of the flow of breathing in and breathing out.

cmp.note: 可以拆成 prāṇa + āyāma（延展），也可以拆成 prāṇa + yama（控制）。英文 breath control 取后者，白话「调息」两边都照顾到。经文给的定义其实是「中断呼吸的流动」，重点在停与慢。
cmp.en: It can be split as prāṇa + āyāma (extension) or prāṇa + yama (control). The English “breath control” takes the latter; the plain Chinese 调息 (tiáoxī, “regulating the breath”) covers both. The text’s own definition is actually “interrupting the flow of breath,” with the emphasis on pausing and slowing.

verses.en: Its working is outward, inward, or held still; observed by place, time, and number, it becomes long and subtle.
The fourth goes beyond the range of outward and inward.
From this, the covering over the light wears away.
And the mind becomes fit for concentration.
Withdrawal of the senses is when the senses, no longer engaged with their objects, seem to take on the mind's own form.

cmp.note: 「往回拉」。英文 withdrawal of the senses、白话「收摄感官」都意译得清楚；注释家的比喻是感官像蜜蜂跟着蜂王，心收回来，感官也跟着收回来。
cmp.en: “Drawing back.” The English “withdrawal of the senses” and the plain Chinese 收摄感官 (shōushè gǎnguān, “gathering in the senses”) both convey the meaning clearly; the commentators’ image is that the senses are like bees following their queen: when the mind withdraws, the senses withdraw with it.

verses.en: From this comes supreme mastery over the senses.

chapters.title: Book 3 · On Powers
chapters.intro: First the last three limbs: concentration, meditation and samadhi, which together on one object are called samyama. Then a long list of special powers samyama on various objects is said to bring, such as knowing past lives, invisibility and walking on air. It warns that these block samadhi; only by not clinging even to them is aloneness reached.

verses.en: Concentration is binding the mind to one place.

cmp.note: 「抓住、托住」。英文 concentration、白话「专注」都是一般用语；原文的画面是把心「绑」在一个点上。
cmp.en: “Holding, supporting.” The English “concentration” and the plain Chinese 专注 (zhuānzhù, “focus”) are both everyday words; the original picture is of tying the mind to a single point.

verses.en: There, an unbroken flow of the same thought is meditation.

cmp.note: 中文「禅」「禅那」就是这个词的音译。英文 meditation 是个大筐，什么静坐都可以叫 meditation；但在瑜伽经里，dhyāna 只是八支中的一步：专注之后、三昧之前，念头不断地流向同一个对象。白话「冥想」也偏宽。
cmp.en: The Chinese 禅 (chán) and 禅那 (chánnà) are transliterations of this very word. The English “meditation” is a catch-all that covers any kind of quiet sitting, but in the Yoga Sūtras, dhyāna is just one of the eight limbs: after concentration and before samādhi, thought flowing unbroken toward a single object. The plain Chinese 冥想 (míngxiǎng, “meditation”) is also rather broad.

verses.en: When that same meditation shines with the object alone, as if emptied of its own form, it is samadhi.
The three together on a single object are called samyama, integrated focus.

cmp.note: 字面是「合在一起抓紧」。白话「总制」是学界译法，一般读者看不懂；英文常见 constraint，本站写 integrated focus，强调是专注、冥想、三昧三步一起作用。
cmp.en: Literally “holding together tightly.” The plain Chinese 总制 (zǒngzhì, “overall control”) is an academic rendering that ordinary readers can’t follow; English often uses “constraint,” while this site says “integrated focus,” stressing that concentration, meditation and samādhi act together as one.

verses.en: By mastering it, the light of insight dawns.
It is applied stage by stage.
These three are more inward than the limbs before them.
Yet even they are outward compared with seedless samadhi.
When the impressions of the outgoing mind are overpowered and the impressions of stilling come forward, and the mind stays with the moment of stilling, this is the transformation of stilling.

cmp.note: 「变成别的样子、演变」，是数论讲物质变化的专门词。英文 transformation、白话「转变」都对；这一章接连讲好几种「转变」，原文是同一个字。
cmp.en: “Becoming something else, evolving,” a technical Sāṃkhya term for change in matter. The English “transformation” and the plain Chinese 转变 (zhuǎnbiàn, “change”) are both correct; this chapter discusses several kinds of transformation in a row, all the same word in the original.

verses.en: Through these impressions, the mind flows on in calm.
When scattering toward everything fades and one-pointedness rises, this is the mind's transformation toward samadhi.
Then again, when the thought that is fading and the thought that is rising are alike, this is the mind's transformation toward one-pointedness.
By this, the transformations of quality, of time-phase, and of condition in the elements and the senses are also explained.

cmp.note: 这里的 dharma 不是「法、教义」，而是「性质、特征」。注释家举例：一块泥可以是泥团、是瓶、是碎片。中文读到「法」字容易想到佛法，白话改成「性质」是对的。
cmp.en: Here dharma doesn’t mean “law, teaching” but “property, characteristic.” The commentators’ example: one lump of clay can be a ball, a pot or shards. Chinese readers seeing 法 (fǎ, the usual rendering of dharma) easily think of the Buddhist Dharma, so the plain Chinese is right to use 性质 (xìngzhì, “property”) instead.

verses.en: The bearer of qualities runs through all its qualities: those that have faded, those now arising, and those not yet nameable.
A difference in sequence is the cause of a difference in transformation.
Through samyama on the three transformations comes knowledge of past and future.
A word's sound, its meaning, and the idea of it get mixed up because each is laid over the others; through samyama on what sets them apart comes understanding of the cries of all creatures.

cmp.note: 指鸟兽的叫声。白话写「一切众生的声音」，英文写 the cries of all creatures；原文说的是听懂动物在叫什么，不只是人的话。
cmp.en: Refers to the calls of birds and animals. The plain Chinese says 一切众生的声音 (yīqiè zhòngshēng de shēngyīn, “the voices of all living beings”), the English “the cries of all creatures”; the original is about understanding what animals are saying, not just human speech.

verses.en: Through directly seeing one's latent impressions comes knowledge of past births.
Through samyama on another's thought comes knowledge of that person's mind.
But not of what that thought is about, since that was not the object of samyama.
Through samyama on the body's visible form, its power to be seen is suspended; with no contact between the light and another's eye, one becomes invisible.
Karma is either quick to ripen or slow; through samyama on it, or through omens, comes knowledge of one's death.

cmp.note: 字面是「最后的终点」。白话「死期」、英文 one's death 都按注释家的理解译出；原文没有直接说「死」字。
cmp.en: Literally “the final end.” The plain Chinese 死期 (sǐqī, “time of death”) and the English “one’s death” both follow the commentators’ reading; the original does not actually use the word “death.”

verses.en: Through samyama on friendliness and the rest comes their strength.
Through samyama on strengths comes the strength of an elephant and the like.
By directing the light of the inner activity, one knows what is subtle, hidden, or far away.
Through samyama on the sun comes knowledge of the worlds.
On the moon: knowledge of how the stars are arranged.
On the pole star: knowledge of their movements.
On the wheel at the navel: knowledge of how the body is arranged.

cmp.note: 「轮」。这是全经唯一一次出现 cakra，只说「脐轮」，并没有后世脉轮体系的七个轮。英文 wheel 照字面，避免把后来的整套说法读进去。
cmp.en: “Wheel.” This is the only appearance of cakra in the entire text, and it mentions only the “navel wheel,” not the later system of seven chakras. The English “wheel” is literal, which avoids reading that later scheme into it.

verses.en: On the hollow of the throat: hunger and thirst fall away.
On the tortoise channel: steadiness.
On the light at the crown of the head: the sight of perfected beings.
Or through flashing intuition, everything.
On the heart: understanding of the mind.

cmp.note: 梵文分得很清楚：对 hṛdaya（心脏，身体上的位置）总制，得到对 citta（心，心理机能）的了解。中文两个都叫「心」，白话只能写「心脏」和「心本身」来区分；英文 heart 和 mind 天然分开。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit makes a clear distinction: samyama on the hṛdaya (the heart, a place in the body) yields understanding of citta (the mind, the mental apparatus). Chinese calls both 心 (xīn), so the plain Chinese has to write 心脏 (xīnzàng, “the heart organ”) and 心本身 (xīn běnshēn, “the mind itself”) to tell them apart; English “heart” and “mind” are naturally separate.

verses.en: Experience is the failure to tell apart the purest part of the mind and the true self, though the two are utterly unmixed; and that experience exists for another's sake. Through samyama on what exists for its own sake comes knowledge of the true self.

cmp.note: 三股绳里最明亮的一股，这里指心最清澈的部分。白话音译「萨埵」，英文写 the purest part of the mind；音译保留了专名，意译让人看得懂，各有取舍。
cmp.en: The brightest of the three strands, here meaning the clearest part of the mind. The plain Chinese transliterates it as 萨埵 (sàduǒ), the English says “the purest part of the mind”; the transliteration keeps the technical name, the paraphrase makes it understandable, each with its trade-off.

verses.en: From this arise flashes of intuition, and heightened hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell.
These are obstacles to samadhi, but powers to the outgoing mind.

cmp.note: 本义是「成就、做成」。白话译「神通」，是借佛教的 abhijñā 旧译，带有神秘色彩；英文 powers 比较平实。这一句很关键：帕坦伽利说这些本事对三昧反而是障碍。
cmp.en: The root meaning is “accomplishment, getting something done.” The plain Chinese renders it 神通 (shéntōng, “supernatural powers”), an old Buddhist rendering of abhijñā with a mystical tint; the English “powers” is plainer. This sūtra is crucial: Patañjali says these abilities are actually obstacles to samādhi.

verses.en: By loosening the causes of bondage and knowing the mind's pathways, the mind can enter another's body.
By mastering the upward breath, one is not caught by water, mud, thorns, and the like, and can rise out of the body at death.

cmp.note: 身体里五种「气」之一，向上运行。白话「上行气」、英文 upward breath 都是意译；这里的「气」不是空气，而是体内的生命力流动。
cmp.en: One of the five “breaths” in the body, the one that moves upward. The plain Chinese 上行气 (shàngxíng qì, “upward-moving qi”) and the English “upward breath” are both interpretive; this “breath” is not air but the flow of life-force within the body.

verses.en: By mastering the balancing breath, one blazes with light.
Through samyama on the link between the ear and space comes divine hearing.

cmp.note: 五大元素之一，声音在其中传播。英文 space、白话「虚空」都不完全对：它不是空无，而是一种很细的物质，旧译又作「以太」。
cmp.en: One of the five great elements, the medium through which sound travels. The English “space” and the plain Chinese 虚空 (xūkōng, “empty space, void”) are both not quite right: it is not emptiness but a very subtle kind of matter, also rendered in older translations as “ether.”

verses.en: Through samyama on the link between the body and space, and by merging with the lightness of cotton fluff, one can travel through the sky.
A fluctuation that works outside the body and is not imagined is called the great bodiless state; from it, the covering over the light wears away.
Through samyama on the elements, in their gross form, their essential nature, their subtle form, their interconnection, and their purpose, comes mastery over the elements.
From this appear the powers of becoming tiny and the rest, perfection of the body, and freedom from being blocked by the elements' properties.

cmp.note: 「变小等等」。原文只举了第一种；白话补出「八种」神通，是按传统的八大成就来补，英文照原文写 and the rest。
cmp.en: “Becoming tiny and so on.” The original names only the first; the plain Chinese adds 八种 (bā zhǒng, “eight kinds”) of powers, following the traditional list of eight great attainments, while the English follows the original with “and the rest.”

verses.en: Perfection of the body is beauty, grace, strength, and diamond-hard firmness.
Through samyama on the senses, in their act of grasping, their essential nature, their sense of "I am," their interconnection, and their purpose, comes mastery over the senses.
From this come the speed of thought, perception without the sense organs, and mastery over primal nature.
Only one who sees the difference between the purest mind and the true self gains mastery over all states of being and knowledge of everything.
By letting go even of this, the seeds of fault are destroyed, and aloneness follows.
When invited by beings in high places, one should feel neither attachment nor pride, for that would bring back what is unwanted.

cmp.note: 「居于高位的」，注释家说是天神。白话直接写「天界的居住者」，英文写 beings in high places，保留了原文的含糊。
cmp.en: “Those in high places,” which commentators say means gods. The plain Chinese writes outright 天界的居住者 (tiānjiè de jūzhùzhě, “dwellers of the heavenly realm”), while the English “beings in high places” keeps the original’s vagueness.

verses.en: Through samyama on the moment and its sequence comes knowledge born of discernment.

cmp.note: 最短的时间单位。白话沿用佛教音译「刹那」，英文写 moment，太日常；原文指不可再分的一瞬。
cmp.en: The smallest unit of time. The plain Chinese keeps the Buddhist transliteration 刹那 (chànà, “an instant”), while the English “moment” is too ordinary; the original means an indivisible instant.

verses.en: From this, two similar things that cannot be told apart by kind, mark, or position can be distinguished.
Knowledge born of discernment is what carries one across: it takes everything as its object, knows its objects in every way, and knows them all at once.

cmp.note: 「渡人过河的」。白话补成「能带人渡过（生死）」，英文写 carries one across，都保留了渡河的比喻，和佛教「到彼岸」用的是同一个画面。
cmp.en: “That which ferries one across the river.” The plain Chinese fills this out as 能带人渡过（生死） (néng dài rén dùguò shēngsǐ, “able to carry one across birth and death”), the English “carries one across”; both keep the river-crossing metaphor, the same image as the Buddhist “reaching the other shore.”

verses.en: When the purest mind and the true self are equal in purity, there is aloneness.

chapters.title: Book 4 · On Aloneness
chapters.intro: On the mind and karma, the force left by past actions: where powers come from, how old habits carry over from life to life, and why the mind cannot see itself. Once one sees the mind is not the self, it turns toward aloneness. The three strands stop changing, and pure awareness rests in its own nature.

verses.en: Powers come from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity, or samadhi.

cmp.note: 「草药」。白话写「药物」，英文写 herbs；注释家说的是一种灵药，不是今天的药品。
cmp.en: “Herbs.” The plain Chinese says 药物 (yàowù, “medicines”), the English “herbs”; commentators mean a kind of elixir, not modern pharmaceuticals.

verses.en: Changing into another kind of being comes from nature flowing in to fill it.
An incidental cause does not drive nature; it only breaks through the barrier, as a farmer does.

cmp.note: 原文只说「像农夫一样」。白话补出「打开田埂让水流过去」，是注释家讲的画面；英文只多写了 breaks through the barrier，读者要自己想到放水入田。
cmp.en: The original says only “like a farmer.” The plain Chinese adds 打开田埂让水流过去 (dǎkāi tiángěng ràng shuǐ liú guòqù, “opening the field ridge to let the water flow through”), the commentators’ image; the English adds only “breaks through the barrier,” leaving readers to picture water being let into the field themselves.

verses.en: Created minds come from the sense of "I am" alone.
Though their activities differ, a single mind sets the many in motion.
Of these, the one born of meditation leaves no store of karma.
A yogi's karma is neither white nor black; for others it is of three kinds.
From this, only those tendencies show up that match the ripening of that karma.

cmp.note: 字面是「熏染的气味」，像衣服沾上了香。白话「习气」借佛教旧译，正好也有「熏」的意思；英文 tendencies 意思对，但没有气味的画面。
cmp.en: Literally “a scent that permeates,” like clothing picking up a fragrance. The plain Chinese 习气 (xíqì, “habit-energies”) borrows an old Buddhist rendering that happens to carry the same sense of being perfumed; the English “tendencies” is correct in meaning but loses the image of scent.

verses.en: Even when separated by birth, place, and time, they follow on without a gap, because memory and latent impressions share one form.
And they have no beginning, because the wish to live is eternal.

cmp.note: 「愿望、祈求」。白话补成「求生的愿望」，英文 the wish to live；原文只有「愿望」一个字，「求生」是按上下文补的。
cmp.en: “Wish, prayer.” The plain Chinese fills this out as 求生的愿望 (qiúshēng de yuànwàng, “the wish to live”), as does the English “the wish to live”; the original has only the single word “wish,” and “to live” is supplied from context.

verses.en: Since they are held together by cause, effect, support, and object, when these are gone, they are gone too.
Past and future exist in their own form, since qualities differ only in their path through time.
These qualities, whether manifest or subtle, are made of the strands of nature.
Because their transformation is unified, a thing is a real thing.
The object is the same, but minds differ; so the two go their separate ways.

cmp.note: 这几句在反驳「外物只是心的产物」的主张，矛头一般认为指向佛教瑜伽行派（唯识）。英文和白话都只能译出论证本身，看不出这是在跟谁辩论。
cmp.en: These sūtras argue against the claim that external objects are merely products of the mind, generally taken to be aimed at the Buddhist Yogācāra (“mind-only”) school. The English and the plain Chinese can only translate the argument itself; you can’t tell who it is arguing with.

verses.en: Nor does an object depend on a single mind; otherwise, when that mind was not knowing it, what would it be?
Because the mind needs to be colored by an object, an object is either known or unknown.
The mind's fluctuations are always known, because their master, the true self, never changes.
The mind does not light itself up, because it is something seen.
And it cannot take in both at the same moment.
If one mind were seen by another, there would be an endless chain of knowing the knower, and memories would be jumbled.
Consciousness does not move from place to place; when the mind takes on its form, the mind becomes aware of its own knowing.

cmp.note: citi（纯粹意识）和 citta（心）只差一个音节，意思却正好相反：一个是不动的觉知，一个是会动的工具。白话「纯粹意识」和「心」分得开，英文 consciousness 和 mind 也分得开，但原文那种「近得危险」的感觉就没了。
cmp.en: Citi (pure consciousness) and citta (mind) differ by only one syllable, yet mean opposite things: one is unmoving awareness, the other a moving instrument. The plain Chinese 纯粹意识 (chúncuì yìshí, “pure consciousness”) and 心 (xīn, “mind”) keep them apart, as do the English “consciousness” and “mind,” but the original’s feeling of the two being dangerously close is lost.

verses.en: The mind, colored by both the seer and the seen, can take in every object.
Though the mind is colored by countless tendencies, it exists for another's sake, because it works by putting things together.

cmp.note: 「斑斓、有花纹的」，也是「图画」。白话「染得斑斓多彩」保留了颜色；英文 colored by 只取了染色，画布的画面没有译出来。
cmp.en: “Variegated, patterned,” and also “a picture.” The plain Chinese 染得斑斓多彩 (rǎn de bānlán duōcǎi, “dyed in brilliant many colors”) keeps the colors; the English “colored by” keeps only the dyeing and loses the image of a painted canvas.

verses.en: For one who sees the difference, the habit of dwelling on one's own self comes to an end.
Then the mind slopes toward discernment and leans toward aloneness.

cmp.note: 两个都是地形词：nimna 是「低洼处」，prāgbhāra 是「向前倾的斜坡」，像水往低处流。英文 slopes、leans 保留了地势；白话「倾向、趋向」就抽象了。
cmp.en: Both are landscape words: nimna is “low ground” and prāgbhāra “a forward-tilting slope,” like water flowing downhill. The English “slopes” and “leans” keep the lie of the land; the plain Chinese 倾向 (qīngxiàng, “to tend toward”) and 趋向 (qūxiàng, “to incline toward”) turn it abstract.

verses.en: In its gaps, other thoughts arise from latent impressions.
Their removal is like that of the afflictions, already described.
For one who seeks no gain even from the highest understanding, discriminating insight is present at all times, and this is the samadhi called the cloud of dharma.

cmp.note: kusīda 是「放债取息的人」，akusīda 就是「不收利息的」：连最高的洞见也不拿来换好处。白话「毫无贪求」、英文 seeks no gain 都意译了，这个放债的比喻没有保留。
cmp.en: A kusīda is a moneylender who charges interest, so akusīda is “one who takes no interest”: not trading even the highest insight for any gain. The plain Chinese 毫无贪求 (háo wú tānqiú, “without any craving”) and the English “seeks no gain” both paraphrase, and the moneylender metaphor is not kept.

cmp.note: 「法云」也是佛教十地中第十地的名字，中文读者会联想到菩萨修行。瑜伽经借用了这个词，但放在自己的体系里，指分辨智一直在场的最后一种三昧。
cmp.en: 法云 (fǎyún, “cloud of dharma”) is also the name of the tenth and final stage of the bodhisattva path in Buddhism, so Chinese readers will think of a bodhisattva’s practice. The Yoga Sūtras borrow the term but place it within their own system, where it means the final samādhi in which discriminating insight is always present.

verses.en: From this, afflictions and karma come to an end.
Then, since knowledge freed of every covering and stain is endless, what is left to know is small.
From this, the strands of nature, their purpose fulfilled, finish their sequence of transformations.
Sequence is what corresponds to moments and is grasped only at the far end of a transformation.
Aloneness is the strands of nature returning to their source, now that they no longer serve any purpose for the true self; or it is the power of consciousness resting in its own true nature.

cmp.note: 全经最后一个字 iti 是「如此、到此为止」，表示讲完了。英文和白话都没有单独译出；这句也呼应了第一章「观者安住在自己的本来面目中」，开头和结尾用的是同一个词 svarūpa。
cmp.en: The very last word of the text, iti, means “thus, so it ends,” marking the close. Neither the English nor the plain Chinese translates it separately. This sūtra also echoes Chapter 1’s “the Seer rests in its own true nature”: the beginning and the end use the same word, svarūpa.
